explanation: The superlative-style comparison converts to the positive degree as 'No other metal is as heavy as lead.'
'Mightier' (comparative) converts to the positive degree as 'The sword is not as mighty as the pen.'
The superlative 'greatest' converts to the positive degree as 'No other virtue is as great as truthfulness.'
'Lighter' (comparative) converts to the positive degree as 'Water is not as light as air.'
The positive-degree comparison converts to the comparative degree as 'Mangoes are sweeter than apples.'
The negative transformation of 'cheap' that preserves the original meaning is 'not expensive', not 'not cheap' (which would reverse the meaning).
The rhetorical question 'When can their glory fade?' asserts that it never can, giving 'Their glory can never fade.'
The affirmative form of 'not sure' is 'doubtful', giving 'I was doubtful of your success.'
'Not always wise' affirmatively becomes 'He is sometimes foolish.'
The interrogative form keeps the original meaning intact: 'Is not virtue its own reward?'
The compound sentence reduces to a simple sentence using a prepositional phrase: 'In spite of being rich, he is not happy.'
Using the correlative conjunction pair 'not only...but also' produces the compound form: 'She is not only beautiful but also intelligent.'
Joining two independent clauses with 'and' produces the compound form: 'He feared that he would be arrested and fled.'
Reducing the second verb to a participle produces the simple form: 'The old man sat in a corner, drinking.'
Joining with the coordinating conjunction 'and' produces the compound form: 'He was ill and didn't attend the party.'
Reducing to a noun clause introduced by 'that' produces the complex form: 'Everybody knows that leprosy is curable.'
Joining with the coordinating conjunction 'and' produces the compound form: 'Buy two shirts and get one free.'
Using the subordinating conjunction 'when' produces the complex form: 'The boy woke up when he heard the noise.'
Reducing the 'as' clause to a participial phrase produces the simple form: 'Deceived by his friends, he lost all hope.'
Using the subordinating conjunction 'if' produces the complex form: 'I will arrest you if you don't speak the truth.'
The adverb 'undeservedly' combines both ideas into one sentence: 'He failed undeservedly.'
The 'too...to' construction combines the two sentences: 'The proposal is too unreasonable to be accepted.'
Reducing 'was tired of work' to the participial phrase 'Tired of work' combines the two sentences using a participle.
The adverb 'honestly' combines the two ideas: 'The minister does his work honestly.'
The infinitive phrase 'to support my big family' expresses purpose, combining the two sentences.
The infinitive phrase 'to do the accounts' expresses purpose, combining the two sentences: 'The manager appointed Zara to do the accounts.'
'The car being expensive' is the absolute phrase combining the two sentences.
The adverbial phrase 'by sunset' combines the two sentences: 'They had not reached their destination by sunset.'
'Clemency' (mercy shown to others) fits the contrast with 'we ourselves are never merciful'.
In context of a 'dreadful occurrence' from food, the element being sought would be the 'toxic' one.
